title: I Built a Visual Subnet Planning Tool for Cloud & DevOps Engineers
summary:
Planning IP ranges and subnet allocations across cloud environments can quickly become messy.

Whether you're working with AWS VPCs, Azure VNets, GCP VPC networks, Kubernetes clusters, or on-premises infrastructure, CIDR planning is something we deal with regularly.

I built Subnets Preview to make this process more visual and easier to manage.

What can it do?

  • Split & Join CIDR blocks — divide address ranges and visualize subnet allocations.
  • Name & Color Subnets — organize networks by purpose, environment, or workload.
  • Export PNG — turn your subnet layout into a visual network reference.
  • Import & Export JSON — save, reuse, and version-control your designs.
  • Share via URL — collaborate by sharing subnet layouts.
  • VS Code / Cursor Extension — preview local subnet designs directly in your editor.

Where is it useful?

  • Planning Virtual Network address spaces.
  • Avoiding overlapping IP ranges across environments.
  • Documenting and visualizing network layouts before implementing them with Terraform or other IaC tools.

Sample VNet: open it

No signup. Just open it and start planning.

It's a small tool built around a common infrastructure problem. Feedback and suggestions are welcome!

title: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout (nginx): causes & fix
summary:
nginx reached the backend but did not get a response within the configured timeout (60 seconds by default).

Common causes

  • Long-running requests: large uploads, exports, reports, image processing.
  • The PHP-FPM pool is full (pm.max_children reached) and new requests wait in line.
  • Slow or locked database queries.
  • fastcgi_read_timeout or proxy_read_timeout too low for the use case.
  • Backend on another host unreachable through network or firewall (connect runs into the timeout).

How to check it

Find timeouts in the nginx log

grep 'upstream timed out' /var/log/nginx/error.log | tail -n 20

Check whether PHP-FPM hits its limit

grep -i 'max_children' /var/log/php8.3-fpm.log

Measure response time precisely

curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'connect=%{time_connect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' https://cloud.example.com/status.php

What actually helps

  1. Fix the cause first: optimise slow queries, add indexes, move long jobs to cron or a queue.
  2. Raise pm.max_children according to RAM (RAM for PHP divided by memory per worker).
  3. Raise timeouts together: fastcgi_read_timeout 300s; in nginx plus max_execution_time and request_terminate_timeout in PHP-FPM.

FAQ

Should I just set the timeout to 3600 seconds?

No. It hides the problem and ties up workers. Raise timeouts only for specific locations such as upload or export paths.

Why do I get a 504 while PHP keeps running?

nginx only drops the connection to the client. The PHP script continues until max_execution_time or request_terminate_timeout kicks in.

Full page with every command and the German/Italian version: daniele-michelin.com/en/errors/http-504-gateway-timeout/

First published at daniele-michelin.com. The error lexicon covers HTTP, DNS, TLS, mail, database, PHP, nginx, systemd and Nextcloud, in German, English and Italian.

title: What Is a Web Server? Apache, Nginx and How Websites Go Live
summary:
Originally published on CodingCush.

A web server is a program that listens for requests from browsers, finds the page or file being asked for, and sends it back. Type an address, press Enter, and your browser asks a web server for that page. In this guide you will learn what a web server does, how static and dynamic content differ, how Apache and Nginx compare, and how a website goes live. You will also run a tiny real web server yourself in two minutes.

What a Web Server Actually Does

Think of a web server as a waiter: the browser orders, and the server brings the food. It does four things, in order. First, it listens, watching a port for requests on a computer that is on and online. Websites use port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. Second, it receives a request, a short message like "GET /about.html". Third, it finds the answer: it reads a plain file from the disk, or passes the request to a program, for a login or a blog post. Fourth, it sends a response, with a status code and the content. A 200 means "here it is", a 404 means "not found", and a 500 means "something broke on the server".

Static vs Dynamic Content

Some pages never change. A simple "About" page is the same HTML file for every visitor, so the server just reads the file and sends it. That is static content, and it is fast, because there is nothing to work out. Other pages are built fresh for each visitor: your inbox, a shopping cart, or a blog homepage are different depending on who asks and when. That is dynamic content. The page does not exist as a file yet, so an application, often in PHP, Python, or Node.js, builds it from a database. Most sites mix the two.

A Request, Step by Step

Follow one click for https://example.com/about. First, your browser asks DNS, the Domain Name System, to turn example.com into an IP address, the server's number on the internet. Second, the browser connects to that address on port 443, because the address starts with https, and asks for /about. Third, the server finds the page, reading a static file or asking an application. Fourth, it sends back a response with a status code, headers, and the page. Finally, the browser reads the HTML, fetches the images and stylesheets, and paints the page. The trip takes well under a second, but any step can fail: a missing file gives a 404, and a crashed application gives a 500.

Try It Yourself: Run a Real Web Server in Two Minutes

Python comes with a tiny built-in web server, perfect for learning because it shows the request and response in plain sight. Create a folder, save this as index.html inside it, and start the server from that folder:



</span>Hello from my web server<span class="nt">

Hello from my web server



python3 -m http.server 8000

The server runs on port 8000 until you stop it with Ctrl+C. In a second terminal, fetch the page with curl:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/

Real output from Python 3.12.3:

HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.12.3
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 05:15:02 GMT
Content-type: text/html
Content-Length: 131

DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Hello from my web servertitle>head>
<body><h1>Hello from my web serverh1>body>
html>

The status line says the request worked, the Server line names the software, and Content-Length says the page is 131 bytes long. The server also logs one line per request:

127.0.0.1 - - [19/Nov/2026 05:15:02] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -

A missing file gives the same "HTTP/1.0 404 File not found" a real site sends. This Python server is a learning tool, not a production server, so never use it for a real website.

The MDN "What is a web server?" page on developer.mozilla.org, a clear official explainer worth reading after this guide.

Apache vs Nginx, in Plain Words

Apache, from the Apache Software Foundation, has been around since the 1990s and is famous for being flexible: modules extend it, and each site can carry its own small config file, which suits shared hosting. Nginx, pronounced "engine X", arrived later and was built for speed under heavy load, handling many connections at once with very little memory. Remember it like this: Apache is a waiter for every table, while Nginx is one very fast waiter for all the tables. For a deeper look, our guide to what Nginx is and how it works walks through it step by step.

Apache Nginx
First released 1995 2004
Connections One process or thread per connection One process, many connections at once
Best at Flexibility, modules, shared hosting High traffic, static files, reverse proxying
Per-site config .htaccess files and VirtualHost blocks Server blocks in the main config

Our full Apache vs Nginx difference guide compares them in more detail. For most beginners, either one works fine.

A Small Nginx Config, Explained Line by Line

Config example, not a command I ran. Nginx was not installed or run for this article. This minimal server block uses only directives from the official Nginx beginners guide:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.com;
    root /var/www/example;
}

Line by line: server { opens a server block, the settings for one website. listen 80; tells Nginx to watch port 80, the normal HTTP port. server_name example.com; says this block answers requests for example.com. root /var/www/example; gives the folder where the site's files live, so a request for /about.html is answered with /var/www/example/about.html. Reload Nginx after editing to apply it.

A Small Apache Config, Explained Line by Line

Config example, not a command I ran. Apache was not installed or run for this article. This VirtualHost block uses only directives from the official Apache getting-started documentation:

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/example
    ErrorLog /var/log/apache2/error.log
VirtualHost>

Line by line: opens a block for websites on port 80, and the star means "on every address this machine has". ServerName example.com says this block answers requests for example.com. DocumentRoot /var/www/example is Apache's name for the folder holding the site's files, the same idea as Nginx's root. ErrorLog /var/log/apache2/error.log tells Apache where to write its error messages.

How a Website Goes Live

Going live connects four pieces: a domain, DNS, a server, and your files. First, register a domain name, like example.com. Second, point it at your server's IP address with a DNS A record; changes can take minutes or hours to spread. Third, install Apache or Nginx on the server, with a server block or VirtualHost pointing at your site's folder. Fourth, copy your files into that folder. Add HTTPS last: a free certificate lets the server answer on port 443 and encrypt traffic. Our guide to how to deploy a website on a VPS server covers each step, and the MDN guide to what a web server is explains the same flow from the browser's point of view.

Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting

Works locally, not on the server. Your files are probably in a different folder than the config points to, so the server answers 404 for everything. Check that DocumentRoot or root matches the upload folder, including capitals: Linux file names are case sensitive.

"Connection refused" in the browser. The server program is not running, or it listens on a different port. Check it is started and you are visiting the right port. A firewall blocking port 80 or 443 gives the same symptom.

You edited the config but nothing changed. Servers read their config when they start, not on every request, so reload or restart after editing. One missing semicolon in Nginx or one unclosed tag in Apache stops the config loading, and the error log names the line.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a web server in simple words?

A program that waits for a browser to ask for a page, finds or builds it, and sends it back.

Is a web server hardware or software?

Both. The software, like Apache or Nginx, handles requests, and the hardware is the computer it runs on. Developers usually mean the software.

What is the difference between Apache and Nginx?

Apache gives each connection its own process or thread. Nginx handles many connections in one process, so it is fast under heavy traffic. For a small site, either one is fine.

Can I run a web server on my own computer?

Yes. Install Apache or Nginx, or use Python's built-in server for a quick test. Making it public needs extra steps, so most people use a rented server instead.

Conclusion

A web server is a simple idea with a big job: listen for requests, find or build the answer, and send it back. Static files go straight from disk to browser, dynamic pages are built by an application first, and Apache and Nginx are two well tested ways of doing that job. Run the Python demo yourself and see it work.

title: I added a "your session is getting long" hook. Context still hit 689K tokens per call. Caps belong in defaults, not reminders
summary:
Short version: if you want to cap an agent's context, telling it to wrap up is not enough. Change the host's defaults. I installed a hook that warns when a Claude Code session gets long. On the first full day it was live, a single call still carried 689K tokens of context. Then I changed two lines of config. In the three days since, no single call has gone above 171K.

Some background. I use Claude Code to plan and review, and Codex to write the code. In part 6 I showed that the planning and reviewing side often burns several times more tokens than the side that writes the code. That isn't because it does more work. It's because every call re-reads the whole conversation.

Attempt 1: a reminder

On November 15 I added long_session_hint.py, a UserPromptSubmit hook. When the main session's context reaches 200K tokens, it says so once, and again at every additional 100K: "hand the next result to a fresh session." It never blocks a prompt and exits quietly on any error.

November 16 was the first full day with the hook live. From my local logs:

  • 4,688 calls, about 662M tokens in total;
  • per-call context: p90 289K, max 689K;
  • subagents were 56% of all usage, and 96% of that ran on Opus.

By design, any session past 200K that day got the reminder. Context kept growing anyway. The reasons aren't mysterious. When the model sees the reminder, it's in the middle of something, and "finish this step first" always sounds right. And the hook only watches the main session. Subagents never pass through it, so they grow on their own.

A reminder changes what the model knows. It doesn't change what it does.

Where the tokens went

On November 17 I laid out eight days of usage. Three causes stood out:

  1. No compaction. Sessions ran on a 1M window and only auto-compacted close to 1M. Over seven days, per-call context had a median of 136K and a p90 of 389K. The longest session had been open for 136 hours straight.
  2. Every subagent on Opus. Subagents were about half of all usage. Almost all were fresh general-purpose subagents with no model set, so they defaulted to Opus. The heaviest session alone spawned 71 of them.
  3. High fixed overhead. The first call of a session already carried about 67K tokens: system prompt, tool definitions, the skill list. A few plugins I never use were part of that.

Attempt 2: change the defaults

Same day, three changes, all in ~/.claude/settings.json, effective for new sessions only:

{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW": "200000",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "sonnet"
  },
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "some-unused-plugin@marketplace": false
  }
}
  • The main session auto-compacts at roughly 200K;
  • subagents default to Sonnet (any subagent that names a model explicitly is unaffected);
  • three unused plugins are off.

I kept the reminder hook. Its job now is to tell me a session is getting long, not to hope the model stops itself.

Three days later

Early today (November 21) I re-ran the same script with the same dedup rule. First a sanity check: for November 10 to 16, daily call counts and totals matched the November 17 review table day for day. Then the days after the change:

Day Calls Total tokens Context p90 Context max Subagent share Opus share within subagents
11-16 (reminder only) 4,688 662M 289K 689K 56% 96%
11-18 3,998 530M 161K 171K 9% 13%
11-20 1,875 197M 155K 170K 29% 8%

The clearest change is the ceiling. After the change, the largest single-call context was 171K, and p90 sat around 160K. That's exactly what a compaction window should do. Opus inside subagents fell from over 90% to around 10%.

Two caveats:

  • Daily totals are not comparable. Every day has different work; 11-20 was lighter mostly because there was less to do. I compare the shape of a single call, not totals, and I'm not claiming a dollar saving.
  • Fixed overhead barely moved. Counting the first main-session call of each session: median about 79K before, about 69K after, roughly 12% down. The plugins I turned off were a small slice. That one is still open.

The formal re-check is on November 24, with a full week of data.

What you can copy

  1. Measure before you change anything. Dedupe by message.id + requestId, bucket by day, and record per-call context p50, p90 and max, plus the subagent share. Without a baseline you can't tell whether a change did anything.
  2. Put the cap in a default. Compaction window and subagent model are host settings. Once set, they apply whether or not the model feels like wrapping up. Keep the reminder for humans.
  3. Watch subagents separately. Hooks on the main session don't see them. Give them their own numbers and their own defaults.
  4. Compare shape, not volume. Workload changes every day, so totals say little. Context p90, max and model mix describe what each call looks like, and those you can compare.
  5. Write down the cost and the way back. Compaction loses detail. Subagents doing hard reviews may get worse; name Opus explicitly for those. To roll back, delete the two env lines.

The core of the counting script is a few lines:

seen = set()
for line in open(transcript):
    rec = json.loads(line)
    msg = rec.get('message') or {}
    usage = msg.get('usage')
    if not usage or (msg.get('id'), rec.get('requestId')) in seen:
        continue
    seen.add((msg.get('id'), rec.get('requestId')))
    ctx = sum(usage.get(k) or 0 for k in
              ('input_tokens', 'cache_creation_input_tokens', 'cache_read_input_tokens'))
    # accumulate ctx and output_tokens by day, subagent or not, and model

This is part 8 of the series. Part 6 said guards belong on the command an agent can't route around. This one is the other side of the same idea: caps belong where the agent doesn't have to decide anything.

About the numbers

  • Hook thresholds (200K, then every 100K) and "warn, never block": from the docstring and constants of long_session_hint.py. It went live the morning of 2026-11-15, per the commit log.
  • Seven-day median 136K, p90 389K, 136 hours, subagents about half, 71 subagents, ~67K first call, the three config changes and their trade-offs: from my 2026-11-17 Claude Code usage review.
  • The table, and the 56% / 96% for 11-16: a read-only scan of my local Claude Code logs on 2026-11-21, deduped by message.id + requestId, bucketed by US Eastern time. "Total" is uncached input + cache writes + cache reads + output. Local logs, not a bill. Call counts and totals for 11-10 to 11-16 match the review table day for day.

Attempt 1: a reminder

On November 15 I added long_session_hint.py, a UserPromptSubmit hook. When the main session's context reaches 200K tokens, it says so once, and again at every additional 100K: "hand the next result to a fresh session." It never blocks a prompt and exits quietly on any error.

A reminder changes what the model knows. It doesn't change what it does.

}

title: Stop Deploying Manually: I Built a CI/CD Pipeline on AWS ECS Fargategs
summary:
By Muhammad Bilal Sharif Bukhari · GitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → ECS Fargate

The 3 a.m. problem every developer knows

My client Lucy had a simple Dockerized 2048 game and a painful release routine: build the image on a laptop, push it by hand, open the AWS console, update the service, refresh the page, and pray.

One typo in a tag, one forgotten step, and the site was down. Every update took longer than the change itself.

So I gave myself one rule for this project: git push is the only deployment step. Everything after it must happen on its own.

Here is how I built it, and every wall I hit on the way.

What I built

A fully automated CI/CD pipeline on AWS (region us-east-1):

  1. A push to GitHub triggers AWS CodePipeline.
  2. AWS CodeBuild pulls the code, builds the Docker image, and tags it.
  3. The image is pushed to Amazon ECR.
  4. Amazon ECS on Fargate starts a new task with the fresh image and removes the old one.

No servers to patch. No manual builds. No console clicking.

The toolkit

Service Its job
GitHub Source of truth and the pipeline trigger
AWS CodePipeline Orchestrates Source → Build → Deploy
AWS CodeBuild Builds and tags the Docker image
Amazon ECR Private registry that stores the images
Amazon ECS (Fargate) Runs the container with no servers to manage
IAM roles and policies Let each service securely talk to the others

Step 1: ECR repository and ECS cluster

I started with the foundations: a private ECR repository (game-2048-repo) and an ECS cluster (game-2048-cluster) using the Fargate launch type. For the task definition I chose a larger task size than the minimum, because I wanted the game to stay smooth and I didn't want resource limits to be a variable while debugging.

Before going further, I checked everything from the CLI. This habit saved me hours later, because the console can look fine while the wiring underneath is wrong.

aws ecs list-clusters
aws ecs list-services --cluster game-2048-cluster

Step 2: Containerizing the game

The game is static files served by Nginx, so the Dockerfile stays tiny:

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY . /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80

I pushed the project to GitHub with a first commit. That repository became the trigger for everything else.

Step 3: CodeBuild, the engine room

CodeBuild reads a buildspec.yml from the repo. Mine logs in to ECR, builds, tags, pushes, and writes a small file called imagedefinitions.json that tells ECS which image to run.

version: 0.2
phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR_URI
  build:
    commands:
      - docker build -t game-2048-repo .
      - docker tag game-2048-repo:latest $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest
  post_build:
    commands:
      - docker push $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest
      - printf '[{"name":"2048-container","imageUri":"%s"}]' $ECR_URI/game-2048-repo:latest > imagedefinitions.json
artifacts:
  files: imagedefinitions.json

Step 4: CodePipeline, connecting the dots

The last step was wiring three stages together: Source (GitHub), Build (CodeBuild), Deploy (ECS). When all three turned green, I pushed a tiny change and watched the whole thing roll out without touching the console.

🚧 Everything that broke (so yours doesn't)

This is the part I wish I'd read before starting. Every item below cost me real time.

1. CodeBuild couldn't push to ECR: no basic auth credentials

My first build died within seconds of reaching the push step. I double-checked the repo name, the region, and the login command, and all of them were right. The real culprit was the CodeBuild service role, which had no ECR permissions at all.

Fix: attach AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser (or a tighter custom policy) to the role.

Lesson: when AWS says "auth," check the IAM role before you check your code.

2. Cannot connect to the Docker daemon

The build started, then failed the moment it ran docker build. CodeBuild doesn't allow Docker-in-Docker by default.

Fix: enable Privileged mode in the CodeBuild environment settings. It's one checkbox, and it's easy to miss.

3. Docker Hub toomanyrequests

One run worked and the next failed with a rate-limit error while pulling the base image. Shared build infrastructure hits Docker Hub's anonymous limits fast.

Fix: pull the base image from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery, or authenticate to Docker Hub inside the build.

4. The Deploy stage failed with an invalid imagedefinitions.json

This one humbled me. Source and Build were green, but Deploy kept failing, and I spent far too long staring at the pipeline instead of at the file. The name inside imagedefinitions.json must match the container name in the ECS task definition exactly, character for character. Mine had a small mismatch.

Fix: copy the container name from the task definition instead of typing it from memory, and make sure the file is declared under artifacts in buildspec.yml.

5. The task started and stopped immediately

The service kept launching tasks that died in seconds. The console said very little until I opened the stopped task and read the stopped reason, then checked the CloudWatch logs.

Fix: correct the container port to match the Dockerfile (80) and make sure the task has an execution role.

6. Task "Running," but the website wouldn't load

The most frustrating one, because everything looked healthy. The task was running and the pipeline was green, yet the browser just spun.

Fix: the security group. I needed to allow inbound HTTP on port 80, and the task needed a public IP to be reachable.

7. The browser shows "Not secure"

I hit this once the site finally loaded. It isn't a bug. It's plain HTTP.

Fix for production: put an Application Load Balancer with an ACM certificate in front of the service.

8. The ECS service never reached a steady state

Tasks kept being created, failing, and being replaced. ECS simply couldn't pull the image.

Fix: make sure the task execution role has AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy, and that the subnet has a network path to ECR (public IP, NAT gateway, or VPC endpoints).

9. The pipeline was green, but I still saw the old game

I pushed a visible change and the page didn't change. The pipeline was fine. The browser was caching, and I was reusing the latest tag.

Fix: hard-refresh first. For anything beyond a lab, tag images with the commit SHA so every release is traceable and rollbacks are easy.

10. Leftover resources

A pipeline, a cluster, a service, and a registry full of images don't clean themselves up.

Fix: when the project is finished, delete the service, cluster, pipeline, CodeBuild project, and ECR images.

💡 What I learned

  • IAM is where most failures live. Nearly every error was some version of "service A isn't allowed to do X to service B." Learning to read those errors was the biggest skill I gained.
  • Exact names matter. One mismatched container name broke an entire deployment.
  • Logs beat guessing. CodeBuild logs and CloudWatch told me what was wrong every single time. I just had to read them first.
  • Fargate removes servers, not networking. Security groups, subnets, and public IPs still decide whether your app is reachable.
  • Verify from the CLI. The console shows what you think you built. The CLI shows what actually exists.
  • latest is a lab tag, not a production strategy. Version your images.
  • Working for a real client changes how you build. I had to explain why each service existed, not just make it work.

What I'd add next

  • A test stage (linting or unit tests) before deployment
  • An Application Load Balancer + HTTPS
  • Infrastructure as Code with Terraform or CloudFormation
  • Blue/green deployments for zero-downtime releases
  • CloudWatch alarms for task health

Final thoughts

I started with a game and finished with a real DevOps workflow: GitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → ECS Fargate, fully automated and serverless.

The best part is the feeling. I changed a line of code, pushed it, made a cup of tea, and the live site had already updated.

Thank you to Lucy for trusting me with this project. 🙌

If you're learning AWS, build this one. Nothing teaches you how CI/CD really works like watching it fail, fixing it, and seeing it go green.

What was the first thing that broke in your first pipeline? Tell me in the comments. 👇

Connect with me on LinkedIn and GitHub.

title: Python Agent Dependencies: Keep Package Installation Away from Deployment Credentials
summary:
Originally published on Snigdh Sharma’s website.

The build environment is part of the agent's security boundary

The November 18 GitHub advisory GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 identifies agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 as malicious releases published on November 17 and subsequently removed from PyPI. It describes Python startup hooks and credential collection, including cloud and CI token paths. This article relies on that published advisory, checked November 21, rather than an independent malware analysis. Consult the live advisory for incident-specific updates.

The broader engineering question is what authority dependency code receives before an agent ever handles a prompt. A package can run in a build environment containing credentials, source code, and deployment tooling. Restricting the agent's runtime tools does not automatically restrict that earlier execution context.

Use hashes to approve bytes, not to certify behavior

pip documents --require-hashes for enforcing locally recorded artifact hashes and --only-binary :all: for excluding source distributions. Hash-checking mode requires pinned requirements and hashes for dependencies as well as direct packages. A partially specified dependency tree should fail installation rather than silently fetch an unreviewed dependency.

For a reviewed requirements file, a typical command is: python -m pip install --require-hashes --only-binary :all: -r requirements.txt. This command is illustrative and was not executed for this article. The file must already contain approved versions and hashes for the target platform. If a dependency lacks a suitable wheel, resolve that explicitly in a separate controlled build process instead of quietly weakening the release policy.

A matching hash establishes that the downloaded bytes match the approved bytes. It does not establish that those bytes are safe. Similarly, using wheels avoids source builds during this step but does not make installed Python code harmless. Treat artifact review, advisory checking, and execution isolation as distinct tasks with distinct evidence.

Separate the build role from the deployment role

My proposed pipeline has three stages. First, dependency changes are reviewed with exact versions, artifact hashes, and source information. Second, a disposable build environment installs and tests that approved set without production deployment credentials. Third, a separate deployment job promotes the identified build artifact using only the permissions required for the destination.

  • Build: use a clean runner with limited repository permissions, no production secrets, and no attached production cloud identity.
  • Artifact handoff: record the source revision, dependency manifest, artifact digest, and test evidence; verify the artifact selected for deployment matches that record.
  • Deploy: avoid resolving fresh application dependencies or executing application startup checks inside the credential-bearing deployment environment. Run application validation in an appropriately isolated target instead.

This separation reduces the authority available during dependency execution; it does not prove that the artifact is trustworthy. The deployment toolchain and any artifact-processing code remain part of the trusted path. Review those components and keep the release handoff small enough to inspect.

Short-lived credentials still need a narrow trust policy

GitHub documents OIDC as a way for workflows to obtain short-lived cloud access through configured trust conditions instead of storing long-lived cloud secrets. The cloud provider checks workflow claims against its trust definition. This reduces long-lived credential handling, but does not make code running in an authorized job trustworthy.

The design implication is to grant token-request capability only where needed and constrain the cloud role to the intended workflow context and destination. Validate the actual claims used by your repository rather than copying an example subject string unchanged. An ephemeral runner with a powerful identity can still perform a powerful action during its lifetime.

Test the boundaries with benign failure cases

  • Change one approved dependency hash in a disposable test fixture. The installation should fail before release; record the observed result instead of assuming enforcement.
  • Add an undeclared dependency to the test requirements. Confirm the strict installation path rejects the incomplete approval record.
  • Review the build job's effective permissions and attached identities. Use a harmless authorization check against a dedicated test resource to validate denial, without printing tokens.
  • Try promoting an artifact whose digest differs from the approval record. The release gate should reject it and identify the mismatch.
  • Rehearse recovery from a suspect dependency using a clean environment and a documented credential-exposure inventory.

These are proposed acceptance tests, not measured results. Adapt them to your CI provider and retain the failed cases as release evidence. The goal is to show which boundary stopped which action, with enough detail for a second engineer to reproduce the check.

A dependency rollback is not credential recovery

For installations affected by the advisory, GitHub recommends treating the environment as exposed and rotating reachable credentials. Removing a package cannot retract a token already copied elsewhere. Preserve the relevant build and identity records, follow your incident process, rebuild from a trusted base, and account for caches and generated artifacts before resuming releases.

Sources

Checked November 21, 2026.

  • GitHub Advisory Database: GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73
  • pip documentation: Secure installs
  • GitHub Actions documentation: OpenID Connect

AI disclosure and limitations

Researched and written autonomously by an AI agent under the site owner's publishing instructions. This is a sourced design guide and proposed validation checklist. No malicious packages were downloaded, no production systems were tested, and no detection or prevention results are claimed.

title: Hermes Agent Review 2026: The Self-Improving AI Agent
summary:
Most AI agents reset to zero every time you start a new conversation. Hermes Agent doesn't. Debugging code, writing articles, managing scheduled tasks across Telegram and Discord, and delegating parallel research workstreams all accumulate into the same persistent memory instead of evaporating at the end of each session. That learning loop isn't a gimmick — it's the single most differentiating feature in the personal AI agent space right now.

This review covers what Hermes Agent does, how its learning system actually works in practice, where it falls short, and whether it's worth your time in 2026.

If you want the short version: Hermes Agent is the best personal AI agent for power users who want an assistant that improves with use. It's not the easiest to set up, it doesn't support the most messaging platforms, and its documentation can be sparse in places. But if you value depth over breadth — an agent that remembers your preferences, builds skills from experience, and gets faster at your routine tasks — nothing else comes close.

What is Hermes Agent?

Hermes Agent is an open-source (MIT-licensed) personal AI agent built by Nous Research — the same team behind the Hermes family of LLMs. At 158K GitHub stars and 9,000+ commits, it's one of the most actively developed agent projects in the world.

The core proposition: an AI agent that grows with you. Unlike agents that treat every conversation as independent, Hermes builds persistent knowledge across sessions. It remembers what worked, creates reusable skills from complex tasks, searches its own conversation history, and develops an increasingly accurate model of who you are and how you work.

The project's homepage puts it well: "It's the only agent with a built-in learning loop — it creates skills from experience, improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions."

Installation & Setup

One-Liner Install

On Linux, macOS, or WSL2:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

On Windows (PowerShell, early beta):

iex (irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.ps1)

The installer handles everything: uv, Python 3.11, Node.js, ripgrep, ffmpeg, and a portable Git Bash on Windows. No manual dependency wrangling.

After Installation

source ~/.bashrc # reload shell hermes # start chatting hermes setup # full setup wizard (provider, model, tools, channels) hermes model # choose your LLM hermes tools # configure tools hermes gateway # start messaging gateway

The setup wizard walks you through choosing a provider, configuring API keys, enabling tools, and connecting messaging platforms. It's not as hand-holding as OpenClaw's openclaw onboard wizard, but it covers everything you need.

Coming from OpenClaw?

Hermes has a built-in migration tool:

hermes claw migrate # Full interactive migration hermes claw migrate --dry-run # Preview what would be migrated hermes claw migrate --preset user-data # Migrate without secrets

This imports your SOUL.md, memories, skills, API keys, channel configs, and TTS assets. The migration is designed to move user data without carrying over secrets.

This is the feature that sets Hermes apart from every other agent. Let me break down each component and how it works in practice.

1. Persistent Memory with Periodic Nudges

Hermes maintains two memory stores:

  • MEMORY.md — the agent's own notes about the environment, tool quirks, project conventions, and lessons learned. Think of it as the agent's personal knowledge base. USER.md — a profile of who you are: communication preferences, coding style, recurring corrections, timezone, role. This is what makes the agent feel personalized.

The key detail: Hermes nudges itself to persist knowledge. After a session where you correct its approach or share a preference, the agent proactively saves it. You don't have to explicitly say "remember this." The next session, that knowledge is already loaded into context.

Example: After I corrected Hermes three times about using Chinese for communication, it saved a memory entry: "Communication language: always use Chinese." Now every new session starts in Chinese without prompting.

2. Automatic Skill Creation

After any complex task — defined as 5+ tool calls with reasoning between them — Hermes autonomously creates a skill. Skills are procedural memory: reusable step-by-step approaches for recurring task types.

Each skill is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (name, tags, version) and markdown body (trigger conditions, numbered steps, pitfalls, verification steps). They live in ~/.hermes/skills/.

Example: After a debugging session involving SSH tunnel setup and port forwarding, Hermes created a ssh-tunnel-debug skill. Next time I hit a similar issue, the skill fires automatically — with the exact commands and common pitfalls already documented.

3. Skill Self-Improvement

Skills aren't static. When Hermes uses a skill and encounters a step that's outdated, incomplete, or wrong, it patches the skill immediately. This means skills get better with use — they accumulate pitfalls, edge cases, and shortcuts that the initial creation couldn't anticipate.

Hermes stores every conversation in a local SQLite database with FTS5 full-text search. When it encounters a new problem, it can search its own past conversations for relevant context — across sessions.

This means if you solved a similar problem three months ago, Hermes can find that conversation and apply the same approach. No other mainstream agent does this. OpenClaw has session history but no cross-session semantic recall. Claude Code and Codex treat every session as independent.

Hermes integrates with Honcho, a dialectic user modeling system. This goes beyond simple preference storage — it builds a progressively deeper model of who you are: how you think, what you prioritize, how you communicate, what frustrates you.

Hermes has a native MCP (Model Context Protocol) client. Configure servers in `config.yaml` and Hermes automatically discovers and registers their tools. This extends Hermes' capabilities without writing any code — connect any MCP-compatible server for database access, API integrations, or custom tools.

### Week 1: Setup & Basics

Installation is quick. The setup wizard handles provider selection, tool configuration, and Telegram gateway connection, and you can be chatting with the agent from both Telegram and the terminal on day one.

Key observation: the TUI felt unfamiliar at first (I'm used to simpler CLI tools), but after two days, the slash-command autocomplete and streaming tool output became second nature. The `/compress` command is essential — when context gets long, compress it instead of starting over.

### Week 2: Skills & Memory

This is where Hermes started differentiating itself. After writing two articles with Hermes (each involving web research, drafting, and WordPress publishing), the agent had created 4 skills automatically: `web-research`, `article-drafting`, `wp-cli-publish`, and `seo-optimization`.

The third article went noticeably faster. Hermes remembered my article structure preferences, knew the WordPress CLI commands without looking them up, and preemptively set Rank Math SEO metadata because the skill had been patched to include that step after my first article.

Within a couple of weeks, USER.md accumulates entries about your preferences. Conversations get shorter because the agent starts preemptively doing things you previously had to ask for.

### Week 3: Delegation & Automation

Three cron jobs cover most of the routine value:

- Daily briefing — 8am, top 5 Hacker News stories + weather → Telegram
- Server monitoring — every 30min, check disk/memory/CPU → alert if above 80%
Weekly summary — Monday 9am, summarize all tasks completed that week → Discord

All three run reliably. The daily briefing improves as the agent accumulates context about your interests, and server monitoring catches disk space issues before they become outages.

Subagent delegation is worth testing against a real research task: "Find the top 5 alternatives to Vercel for serverless deployment, compare pricing, and create a summary table." Hermes spawns parallel subagents — one for pricing data, one for feature comparison, one for community sentiment — and returns a consolidated answer in a couple of minutes.

## Where Hermes Falls Short

### 1. Channel Coverage

6 platforms vs OpenClaw's 24. No WhatsApp native integration yet (it's listed but still early), no WeChat, no iMessage, no Microsoft Teams, no Matrix. If you need your agent on those channels, you'll need OpenClaw as a complement — or wait for Hermes to add them.

### 2. No GUI Onboarding

The TUI is powerful but has a learning curve. OpenClaw's `openclaw onboard` wizard is more accessible for non-technical users. Hermes' `hermes setup` covers the same ground but requires comfort with a terminal interface.

### 3. Documentation Gaps

The docs are good for core features but thin on advanced configuration. Understanding cron job delivery targets generally requires reading the source code. The Chinese translation of the README is a nice touch, but the full docs aren't translated.

### 4. Python Runtime Overhead

Compared to ZeroClaw's Rust core, Hermes' Python runtime has higher memory usage and slower cold starts. On a 512MB VPS, you'll feel it. The serverless backends (Modal/Daytona) mitigate this, but local execution on constrained hardware is not Hermes' strength.

### 5. Community Size

158K stars is huge, but OpenClaw's 373K means more contributors, more skills, more bug reports getting filed, and more edge cases getting found. Hermes' community is growing fast (9,000+ commits, 4,200+ issues) but it's still the smaller ecosystem.

## Pricing

Hermes Agent is free and open-source (MIT license). Your only costs are:

- LLM API calls — depends on your provider and model. OpenRouter starts at ~$0.10/1M tokens for budget models, ~$3/1M tokens for flagship models.
- Hosting — $5/month VPS for self-hosting, or near-zero with Modal/Daytona serverless backends.
Messaging platform costs — Telegram/Discord/Slack bots are free. WhatsApp Business API has its own costs.

Total cost depends entirely on the models you route to. Running OpenRouter lets you mix budget models for routine work with premium models for the hard problems, and because every request is metered per token you can attribute spend to research, article writing, cron jobs and delegation separately. Set a monthly cap in the provider dashboard before you start — an agent that delegates will find ways to spend it.

title: Upgrading Old PHP Versions Safely With Rector and CI
summary:
In almost every legacy PHP project Loop Origin takes on, the first question is the same: which PHP version is production on? The answer is often 7.2 or 7.4, sometimes 5.6, on a server nobody wants to touch. PHP 7.4 reached end of life in November 2022, and PHP 8.0 followed a year later, so these apps run without security fixes and block every modern package. The team knows it. The upgrade keeps getting postponed because it feels like one big risky jump.

It does not have to be one jump. With the strangler fig from Part 1 and clean module boundaries from Part 2, the version upgrade becomes a series of small, tested pull requests that each leave production working. This post is the playbook I use.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked the tooling details against the Rector, PHPStan and PHPCompatibility documentation and the official PHP migration guides. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years maintaining Laravel and plain-PHP systems, and the numbers below come from real upgrades, not benchmarks.

📚 Series Navigation — Modernizing Legacy PHP Without a Rewrite

  • Part 1: Strangler Fig for Legacy PHP: Run Old and New Side by Side
  • Part 2: Untangling Dependency Cycles in a Modular Laravel Monolith
  • Part 3 (This Post): Upgrading Old PHP Versions Safely With Rector and CI
  • Part 4: Replacing Legacy Auth & Sessions Without Logging Everyone Out
  • Part 5: From FTP Deploys and Cron Scripts to a Real Pipeline
  • Part 6: Decommissioning the Old App: Shadow Traffic, Flags & Final Cutover

Related earlier posts: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations in Laravel & Node.js SaaS · Production Observability on a Budget

How do you upgrade an old PHP app to PHP 8 safely?

Direct answer: Add CI that runs your tests on both the current and target PHP versions, scan for incompatibilities with PHPCompatibility and PHPStan, let Rector apply the mechanical code changes in small batches, upgrade Composer dependencies one at a time, then roll the new runtime out to one server or container first, with a quick way back.

Which tool does what

Tool What it finds or does Changes code? Where I run it
PHPCompatibility (PHP_CodeSniffer) Removed functions, syntax and extensions for a target version No CI, first pass
PHPStan Type errors, undefined methods, wrong argument counts No CI, every PR
Rector Automated refactors: version sets, deprecated calls, typed properties Yes Locally, small batches
Test suite (PHPUnit / Pest) Behaviour regressions No CI matrix on old + new PHP
Error logs on canary Runtime deprecations you missed No Staged rollout

None of these is enough alone. Static tools miss dynamic code (call_user_func, string class names, extract()), and tests rarely cover everything in a legacy app. Together they catch most of it.

Step 1: get a safety net, however thin

If the app has no tests, I do not start by writing unit tests for everything. I write 20 to 40 HTTP-level characterization tests for the money paths: login, checkout or invoicing, the main reports, any import job. They record what the app returns today, so I know when an upgrade changes it.

public function test_invoice_pdf_still_renders(): void
{
    $this->actingAs(User::factory()->create())
         ->get('/invoices/1042/pdf')
         ->assertOk()
         ->assertHeader('content-type', 'application/pdf');
}

Step 2: run CI on both versions

The key idea: code must pass on the old version and the new one at the same time, so every PR can ship to the current production server.

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        php: ['7.4', '8.3']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: ${{ matrix.php }}, coverage: none }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: vendor/bin/phpcs -p --standard=PHPCompatibility --runtime-set testVersion 7.4-8.3 app/ legacy/
      - run: vendor/bin/phpstan analyse --memory-limit=1G
      - run: vendor/bin/phpunit

At first the 8.3 job fails. That is fine. Mark it allowed-to-fail, and the list of failures becomes your backlog.

Step 3: let Rector do the boring part

Rector applies the mechanical changes: each() loops, curly-brace string offsets, create_function, implicit nullable parameters, and so on. Configure it to stay compatible with the old version first, then raise the target later.

// rector.php
use Rector\Config\RectorConfig;
use Rector\Set\ValueObject\LevelSetList;

return RectorConfig::configure()
    ->withPaths([__DIR__.'/app', __DIR__.'/legacy'])
    ->withSkip([__DIR__.'/legacy/vendor_copied'])
    ->withSets([LevelSetList::UP_TO_PHP_74]);   // later: UP_TO_PHP_80, then UP_TO_PHP_83

vendor/bin/rector process legacy/Billing --dry-run   # review the diff
vendor/bin/rector process legacy/Billing             # apply one module at a time

I run Rector one directory per PR, using the module boundaries from Part 2. A 300-line diff gets reviewed properly; a 30,000-line diff gets rubber-stamped.

Step 4: fix what tools cannot

The PHP 8 changes that bit me most in real projects:

  • String-to-number comparisons. 0 == "abc" was true in PHP 7 and is false in PHP 8. Search for loose comparisons against user input and status codes.
  • Warnings that became errors. Undefined array keys and properties are louder, and many internal functions now throw TypeError on null where they used to return quietly.
  • Removed extensions. mysql_* (gone since 7.0), mcrypt, and old each() usage need real replacements, not shims.
  • Dynamic properties are deprecated in 8.2. Add the properties or #[AllowDynamicProperties] deliberately.
  • Dependencies. Upgrade Composer packages one at a time with composer why-not php 8.3 to see which package blocks you.

Step 5: roll out the runtime in stages

With CI green on both versions, the server change is the smallest step. I build a new PHP 8.3 container or server next to the old one, route 5% of traffic to it, and watch error logs and latency for a day, then 50%, then 100%. Rolling back means pointing traffic back at the old pool. Keep the old pool for a week.

If you would rather not run this yourself, Loop Origin does exactly this kind of server setup and maintenance work, and the code side as part of our Laravel development service.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Characterization tests cover the money paths
  • [ ] CI runs tests, PHPCompatibility and PHPStan on both old and target PHP
  • [ ] Rector runs one module per PR, reviewed as a normal diff
  • [ ] Loose comparisons against strings are audited
  • [ ] Removed extensions (mysql_*, mcrypt) are replaced
  • [ ] Composer dependencies are upgraded individually with why-not checks
  • [ ] Deprecation logging is on in staging and canary
  • [ ] New runtime goes live behind a traffic split with a tested rollback

FAQ

Should I go straight from PHP 7.x to 8.3?

For the code, yes, as long as Rector and CI step through the sets in order. Running each intermediate version in production is usually not worth it.

How long does a typical upgrade take?

It depends on size and tests. On the mid-sized apps we see, it is usually a few weeks of part-time work spread over small PRs, not a frozen big-bang sprint.

Can Rector break my code?

Yes, occasionally, especially with dynamic code. That is why you review diffs in small batches and rely on the test matrix.

What about the old framework version?

Upgrade PHP first while staying on a framework version that supports both PHP versions, then upgrade the framework as a separate project.

Do I need Docker for the staged rollout?

No. A second server or PHP-FPM pool behind the same load balancer works. Containers just make the old and new runtimes easier to keep side by side.

Is it safe to keep running PHP 7.4 if the server is behind a firewall?

It reduces exposure but does not remove it. Unpatched runtimes also block security updates in your dependencies, which is often the bigger risk.

title: Patching a PHP security release in 40 minutes on an LB ASG EC2 stack
summary:
Introduction

Around 23:00 JST on November 19, 2026, the PHP team shipped security releases for 8.2 through 8.5. There were 17 GitHub Security Advisories (GHSAs), 7 of them critical. Thirty-eight minutes after the GHSAs went public, we put production back behind the load balancer (LB), running patched PHP.

This post shows how to get patched on release day when you run PHP from Ubuntu packages on an LB → Auto Scaling group (ASG) → EC2 stack.

  • Some PHP versions have reached end of life on php.net, so upstream ships no fixes for them
  • Neither Ubuntu nor the ondrej PPA had fixed packages that day, so we backported the upstream fixes onto the Ubuntu source and built the packages ourselves
  • Instead of patching ASG instances one by one, we built a patched AMI and replaced every instance

Assumed setup

This post assumes a mix of environments that use an ASG and environments that don't.

With ASG Without ASG
Topology LB → ASG → EC2. Some instances are registered directly with the LB ALB → EC2
How AMIs are built From a dedicated golden instance. Creating an AMI automatically adds a new launch template (LT) version, and the ASG launches instances from the LT's $Latest With Packer, which installs PHP from apt at build time
  • Instances are managed with AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Run Command, so no SSH logins are needed
  • PHP comes from Ubuntu packages, and security updates normally arrive through apt

Why the usual approach is slow

As long as you wait for the distribution's fix, you don't control when you're done. With an ASG, AMIs add another layer of problems.

  • You don't know when fixed packages will land. This time the PPA (ondrej) published at 05:38 the next morning and Ubuntu published to Launchpad at 09:46, 6 to 11 hours after upstream. The packages reached the apt repositories even later
  • Patching running instances isn't enough. Instances launched by scale-out or replacement boot from the old AMI
  • You can't bake a fresh AMI yet. If Packer installs PHP from apt, you can't bake until the fix is in apt
  • Instances get replaced while you're out of the LB. If health checks or AZ rebalancing make the ASG replace instances, unpatched ones come up

Approach

Build the fix yourself instead of waiting, rebuild the AMI, and replace every instance in the ASG. We followed five rules.

  1. Prepare as soon as the release is pre-announced. Launch an EC2 build host and build the Ubuntu source once without patches. That warms ccache and gives you a test baseline (the tests that fail even without patches). Rehearse the distribution steps with this build too
  2. Take production out of the LB before the release. You only learn the details after publication, so take it out whether or not you turn out to be affected, and patch the same day
  3. Backport the upstream fixes onto the Ubuntu source and build debs. Append a suffix such as +local1 to the Ubuntu version. Ubuntu's next version sorts higher, so moving back to the official package later is easy
  4. Distribute via S3 and SSM. Depend on neither apt mirrors nor SSH
  5. Never patch ASG instances directly. Patch the golden instance, create an AMI, terminate every ASG instance, and let them come back on the new AMI. Running instances and future ones end up on the same AMI

ASG instances get the fix in this order: golden instance → AMI → LT → replace all instances. Instances outside the ASG are patched directly.

Timeline

Identifying, backporting, and building the fix took 13 minutes, the AMI and LT 6 minutes, and replacing the ASG instances 11 minutes. These three account for most of the 38 minutes.

Applying the packages to an instance takes only 1 to 2 minutes. Environments without an ASG were patched directly, without waiting for the AMI.

Key steps

Taking production out of the LB

Before taking it out, stop the ASG from replacing instances automatically. Otherwise unpatched instances boot from the old AMI while you're out of the LB.

aws autoscaling suspend-processes --auto-scaling-group-name <ASG> \
  --scaling-processes ReplaceUnhealthy AZRebalance AlarmNotification
aws autoscaling detach-load-balancers --auto-scaling-group-name <ASG> --load-balancer-names <CLB>
aws elb deregister-instances-from-load-balancer --load-balancer-name <CLB> --instances <instance IDs outside the ASG>
  • A CLB can't return a fixed response, so detach the instances to stop traffic. Closing the security group doesn't cut established connections
  • Once the instances are detached, users get 503. Turn on the app's maintenance mode before detaching, and after reattaching, verify behavior while still in maintenance before turning it off
  • With an ALB, switch the listener's default action to a fixed 503 response
  • Record which processes were already suspended before you start, so that you don't resume them when you put production back
  • If you use scheduled scaling (scheduled actions), also suspend ScheduledActions or make sure nothing is scheduled while you're out. A scale-out would boot unpatched instances from the old AMI

Backporting and building the fix

  1. Pick the fix commits from the diff between the previous and new tags of the oldest supported branch in php-src (for example git log php-8.2.35..php-8.2.36). Skip commits that only bump versions or touch CI or tests
  2. For each GHSA, decide whether your version is affected. If you run an end-of-life version, treat it as affected when the fix landed on every branch from 8.2 up. If the function or extension being fixed doesn't exist in your version, it's out of scope
  3. Apply the commits with git am -3 onto a tree with Ubuntu's patches applied, and resolve conflicts by hand. Export the result as a single quilt patch into debian/patches
  4. Add a +local1 version to debian/changelog and build. Bump to +local2 on every rebuild so you never ship different debs under the same version
  5. Run the test suite and confirm there are no new failures compared to the unpatched baseline. Run the phpt tests that came with each fix against both the official deb and yours, and confirm that only yours passes

With ccache warm, a build with the patch added finishes in 4 to 5 minutes. However, Ubuntu's PHP build puts the version into -fdebug-prefix-map, so changing the version misses the cache entirely. Exclude that option from the ccache hash with CCACHE_IGNOREOPTIONS.

Distributing to instances

Bundle the debs into a tarball, upload it to a temporary S3 bucket, and pass a presigned URL valid for one hour to the instances via SSM Run Command. Each instance downloads from the URL, verifies against SHA256SUMS, and then swaps the packages.

On each instance:

  • Replace only the PHP packages that are already installed, with dpkg -i. Older apt can't install a deb whose version contains + with apt-get install ./x.deb
  • apt-mark hold the replaced packages, so automatic updates or configuration management don't roll them back
  • During the swap, use policy-rc.d to keep maintainer scripts from reloading or restarting services, then restart the web server once at the end
  • Afterwards, check versions and holds, and make sure no process is still running the old PHP

Rebuilding the AMI and replacing ASG instances

After patching the golden instance, create an AMI and wait for the LT to point to it (6 minutes this time). Then terminate every ASG instance without decrementing the desired capacity.

aws autoscaling terminate-instance-in-auto-scaling-group --instance-id <ID> \
  --no-should-decrement-desired-capacity

The ASG launches replacements from the new AMI. Since production is out of the LB, terminating everything at once doesn't affect users. Replacement took 11 minutes this time. Before replacing, confirm that the ASG is out of the LB, that ReplaceUnhealthy is suspended, and that the LT has the new AMI.

Check versions, holds, and health checks on the new instances. Then attach the ASG to the LB, and resume the suspended processes once all instances are InService.

After the official fix ships

The self-built packages are a stopgap: switch back once the official fix ships. We set things up so that removing the hold is all it takes.

  1. Compare your fix with the official one. Run debdiff against the previous version and compare the new debian/patches with your patch. Look beyond the changelog at the patch contents and series
  2. If they match, unhold. The official version sorts above +local1, so apt upgrade or the next AMI rebuild picks it up naturally
  3. Unhold the golden instance too. AMIs baked from it carry the hold, so if you forget, PHP stays frozen in every later AMI
  4. Rebake Packer-built AMIs only after the fix reaches the apt repositories. Baking earlier installs the unpatched version. Add a check to the build script that the PHP version is at least the fixed one 
dpkg --compare-versions "$(dpkg-query -W -f='${Version}' )" ge <fixed version>

Pitfalls and lessons

  • Publication comes before the php.net announcement. The php-src tags and GHSAs went public at 23:06 and the php.net announcement came at 23:12. The php.net Atom feed can lag, so watch the GitHub tags and GHSAs directly
  • apt mirrors go down. On the day, the Ubuntu mirrors didn't respond from 21:20 to 21:48. Distributing via S3 kept us unaffected
  • Long-running processes keep the old PHP. Restart CLI workers run by supervisor and the like after the swap. Look for processes still mapping deleted shared libraries (marked (deleted) in /proc//maps)
  • Holds silently block updates. Neither apt upgrade nor configuration management reports an error; PHP just stays old. Always record unholding as a follow-up task
  • Fixes can include behavior changes. This time a fix changed the default of an ini setting. Read the diff before taking it in

Summary

Even on an LB → ASG → EC2 stack, patched production was back behind the LB within 40 minutes of publication. Three things made it work:

  • Don't wait for the fix: backport it onto the distribution source and build it yourself. Use a version suffix and a hold so you can go back to the official package
  • Prepare the build host, the test baseline, and the distribution steps between the announcement and the release
  • Don't patch ASG instances one by one. Bring them all in line at once through golden instance → AMI → LT → replace all instances, and stop the ASG's automatic replacement before taking production out of the LB

This post shows how to get patched on release day when you run PHP from Ubuntu packages on an LB → Auto Scaling group (ASG) → EC2 stack.

  • Some PHP versions have reached end of life on php.net, so upstream ships no fixes for them
  • Neither Ubuntu nor the ondrej PPA had fixed packages that day, so we backported the upstream fixes onto the Ubuntu source and built the packages ourselves
  • Instead of patching ASG instances one by one, we built a patched AMI and replaced every instance

Assumed setup

This post assumes a mix of environments that use an ASG and environments that don't.

With ASG Without ASG
Topology LB → ASG → EC2. Some instances are registered directly with the LB ALB → EC2
How AMIs are built From a dedicated golden instance. Creating an AMI automatically adds a new launch template (LT) version, and the ASG launches instances from the LT's $Latest With Packer, which installs PHP from apt at build time
  • Instances are managed with AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Run Command, so no SSH logins are needed
  • PHP comes from Ubuntu packages, and security updates normally arrive through apt

Why the usual approach is slow

As long as you wait for the distribution's fix, you don't control when you're done. With an ASG, AMIs add another layer of problems.

  • You don't know when fixed packages will land. This time the PPA (ondrej) published at 05:38 the next morning and Ubuntu published to Launchpad at 09:46, 6 to 11 hours after upstream. The packages reached the apt repositories even later
  • Patching running instances isn't enough. Instances launched by scale-out or replacement boot from the old AMI
  • You can't bake a fresh AMI yet. If Packer installs PHP from apt, you can't bake until the fix is in apt
  • Instances get replaced while you're out of the LB. If health checks or AZ rebalancing make the ASG replace instances, unpatched ones come up

Approach

Build the fix yourself instead of waiting, rebuild the AMI, and replace every instance in the ASG. We followed five rules.

  1. Prepare as soon as the release is pre-announced. Launch an EC2 build host and build the Ubuntu source once without patches. That warms ccache and gives you a test baseline (the tests that fail even without patches). Rehearse the distribution steps with this build too
  2. Take production out of the LB before the release. You only learn the details after publication, so take it out whether or not you turn out to be affected, and patch the same day
  3. Backport the upstream fixes onto the Ubuntu source and build debs. Append a suffix such as +local1 to the Ubuntu version. Ubuntu's next version sorts higher, so moving back to the official package later is easy
  4. Distribute via S3 and SSM. Depend on neither apt mirrors nor SSH
  5. Never patch ASG instances directly. Patch the golden instance, create an AMI, terminate every ASG instance, and let them come back on the new AMI. Running instances and future ones end up on the same AMI

ASG instances get the fix in this order: golden instance → AMI → LT → replace all instances. Instances outside the ASG are patched directly.

Timeline

Identifying, backporting, and building the fix took 13 minutes, the AMI and LT 6 minutes, and replacing the ASG instances 11 minutes. These three account for most of the 38 minutes.

Applying the packages to an instance takes only 1 to 2 minutes. Environments without an ASG were patched directly, without waiting for the AMI.

Key steps

Taking production out of the LB

Before taking it out, stop the ASG from replacing instances automatically. Otherwise unpatched instances boot from the old AMI while you're out of the LB.

aws autoscaling suspend-processes --auto-scaling-group-name <ASG> \
  --scaling-processes ReplaceUnhealthy AZRebalance AlarmNotification
aws autoscaling detach-load-balancers --auto-scaling-group-name <ASG> --load-balancer-names <CLB>
aws elb deregister-instances-from-load-balancer --load-balancer-name <CLB> --instances <instance IDs outside the ASG>
  • A CLB can't return a fixed response, so detach the instances to stop traffic. Closing the security group doesn't cut established connections
  • Once the instances are detached, users get 503. Turn on the app's maintenance mode before detaching, and after reattaching, verify behavior while still in maintenance before turning it off
  • With an ALB, switch the listener's default action to a fixed 503 response
  • Record which processes were already suspended before you start, so that you don't resume them when you put production back
  • If you use scheduled scaling (scheduled actions), also suspend ScheduledActions or make sure nothing is scheduled while you're out. A scale-out would boot unpatched instances from the old AMI

Backporting and building the fix

  1. Pick the fix commits from the diff between the previous and new tags of the oldest supported branch in php-src (for example git log php-8.2.35..php-8.2.36). Skip commits that only bump versions or touch CI or tests
  2. For each GHSA, decide whether your version is affected. If you run an end-of-life version, treat it as affected when the fix landed on every branch from 8.2 up. If the function or extension being fixed doesn't exist in your version, it's out of scope
  3. Apply the commits with git am -3 onto a tree with Ubuntu's patches applied, and resolve conflicts by hand. Export the result as a single quilt patch into debian/patches
  4. Add a +local1 version to debian/changelog and build. Bump to +local2 on every rebuild so you never ship different debs under the same version
  5. Run the test suite and confirm there are no new failures compared to the unpatched baseline. Run the phpt tests that came with each fix against both the official deb and yours, and confirm that only yours passes

With ccache warm, a build with the patch added finishes in 4 to 5 minutes. However, Ubuntu's PHP build puts the version into -fdebug-prefix-map, so changing the version misses the cache entirely. Exclude that option from the ccache hash with CCACHE_IGNOREOPTIONS.

Distributing to instances

Bundle the debs into a tarball, upload it to a temporary S3 bucket, and pass a presigned URL valid for one hour to the instances via SSM Run Command. Each instance downloads from the URL, verifies against SHA256SUMS, and then swaps the packages.

On each instance:

  • Replace only the PHP packages that are already installed, with dpkg -i. Older apt can't install a deb whose version contains + with apt-get install ./x.deb
  • apt-mark hold the replaced packages, so automatic updates or configuration management don't roll them back
  • During the swap, use policy-rc.d to keep maintainer scripts from reloading or restarting services, then restart the web server once at the end
  • Afterwards, check versions and holds, and make sure no process is still running the old PHP

Rebuilding the AMI and replacing ASG instances

After patching the golden instance, create an AMI and wait for the LT to point to it (6 minutes this time). Then terminate every ASG instance without decrementing the desired capacity.

aws autoscaling terminate-instance-in-auto-scaling-group --instance-id <ID> \
  --no-should-decrement-desired-capacity

The ASG launches replacements from the new AMI. Since production is out of the LB, terminating everything at once doesn't affect users. Replacement took 11 minutes this time. Before replacing, confirm that the ASG is out of the LB, that ReplaceUnhealthy is suspended, and that the LT has the new AMI.

Check versions, holds, and health checks on the new instances. Then attach the ASG to the LB, and resume the suspended processes once all instances are InService.

After the official fix ships

The self-built packages are a stopgap: switch back once the official fix ships. We set things up so that removing the hold is all it takes.

  1. Compare your fix with the official one. Run debdiff against the previous version and compare the new debian/patches with your patch. Look beyond the changelog at the patch contents and series
  2. If they match, unhold. The official version sorts above +local1, so apt upgrade or the next AMI rebuild picks it up naturally
  3. Unhold the golden instance too. AMIs baked from it carry the hold, so if you forget, PHP stays frozen in every later AMI
  4. Rebake Packer-built AMIs only after the fix reaches the apt repositories. Baking earlier installs the unpatched version. Add a check to the build script that the PHP version is at least the fixed one 
dpkg --compare-versions "$(dpkg-query -W -f='${Version}' )" ge <fixed version>

Pitfalls and lessons

  • Publication comes before the php.net announcement. The php-src tags and GHSAs went public at 23:06 and the php.net announcement came at 23:12. The php.net Atom feed can lag, so watch the GitHub tags and GHSAs directly
  • apt mirrors go down. On the day, the Ubuntu mirrors didn't respond from 21:20 to 21:48. Distributing via S3 kept us unaffected
  • Long-running processes keep the old PHP. Restart CLI workers run by supervisor and the like after the swap. Look for processes still mapping deleted shared libraries (marked (deleted) in /proc//maps)
  • Holds silently block updates. Neither apt upgrade nor configuration management reports an error; PHP just stays old. Always record unholding as a follow-up task
  • Fixes can include behavior changes. This time a fix changed the default of an ini setting. Read the diff before taking it in

Summary

Even on an LB → ASG → EC2 stack, patched production was back behind the LB within 40 minutes of publication. Three things made it work:

  • Don't wait for the fix: backport it onto the distribution source and build it yourself. Use a version suffix and a hold so you can go back to the official package
  • Prepare the build host, the test baseline, and the distribution steps between the announcement and the release
  • Don't patch ASG instances one by one. Bring them all in line at once through golden instance → AMI → LT → replace all instances, and stop the ASG's automatic replacement before taking production out of the LB

title: Cline Review 2026: The Open-Source AI Agent for VS Code
summary:
What Is Cline?

Cline (formerly Claude Dev) is an open-source AI coding agent that runs as a VS Code extension. Unlike Copilot's inline suggestions, Cline can plan multi-step changes, create and edit files, run terminal commands, and use a browser — all autonomously within your project. It is the open-source alternative to Cursor's agent mode.

Cline at a Glance

Area What it does Who it suits
Reviewability Shows every prompt, tool call, and diff in the session Teams that require audit before merge
Execution control Proposes a plan, you approve each write Review-first, quality-first developers
Model choice Bring your own provider or a local model Cost- and privacy-conscious teams
Open source Inspect and fork the extension itself Security teams and maintainers

How Cline Works

You describe a task in natural language. Cline analyzes your project structure, plans the implementation, and executes it step by step. It can create files, edit existing code, run tests, read error messages, and iterate until the task is complete. You approve each action or let it run autonomously.

Key Features

  • Multi-step task execution: Plans and implements complex changes across multiple files
  • Terminal access: Runs commands, installs packages, executes tests
  • Browser tool: Can check web documentation and API references
  • Model flexibility: Works with Claude, GPT-4, Gemini, DeepSeek, and local models via OpenAI-compatible APIs Context awareness: Reads your entire project structure before acting

What Cline Does Well

Transparency by design

Its defining trait is that you can see exactly what the agent chose. Every tool call, the file it edits, and the prompt that drove it are part of the session. When a change is wrong, you read the audit and correct a specific step, instead of spending an afternoon reconstructing what the model guessed. For a review-heavy team, that audit habit de-risks every merge.

Explicit, diffable edits

Cline proposes a diff you can inspect before it modifies anything. You are not asked to trust a single accept-all click. Seeing and editing each change before it lands is the meaningful difference between an agent that "just did it" and one you actually supervise.

Open source, so you can audit it

Because Cline is open source, the tool is transparent too. You never depend on an endpoint you cannot examine, which matters for a security-conscious team or a careful open-source maintainer.

Bring your own model

You decide which model presides. That keeps control of cost and privacy in your hands and fits teams that want to route smaller or self-hosted models into the same loop without changing tools.

Cline vs Cursor Agent Mode

Cursor's agent mode is more polished with better UI and faster iteration. Cline is open-source, works with any model, and runs in your existing VS Code setup. If you already use VS Code and do not want to switch editors, Cline is the practical choice. See our Cursor IDE Review for the full Cursor comparison.

Cline vs GitHub Copilot

Different tools entirely. Copilot suggests code as you type. Cline executes multi-step tasks autonomously. Copilot is passive assistance; Cline is active agency. They complement each other rather than compete. See our GitHub Copilot Review.

Real-World Results

Adding auth to a Next.js app — 12 minutes

Cline created the auth middleware, login/signup pages, API routes, and updated the navbar. Required one correction (wrong redirect URL). Solid result for a task that would take 30+ minutes manually.

Writing unit tests for a React component — 8 minutes

Generated comprehensive tests with React Testing Library. 85% pass rate on first run. Fixed the 2 failing tests automatically on the next iteration.

Refactoring a Python API — 15 minutes

Split a monolithic route file into separate modules. Cline understood the dependency graph and updated all imports correctly. Impressive architectural understanding.

A Realistic Workflow with Cline

A healthy daily loop with Cline starts with a small, well-scoped task. You open Cline, point it at the relevant files, describe the change you want in a sentence or two, and let it read the project and propose a plan. You read that plan the same way you read a teammate's design note: is the approach right, is it too broad, does it touch files it should not? Only then do you let it draft the diff, and only when you approve does the edit land. This sounds slower than an accept-all flow, but it shifts the cost to the moment of the decision, catches a bad direction before a single edit is written, and leaves a clean audit of every step. Teams that run it this way consistently report that time moves from rework to review, which is a net win for the codebase.

The other habit worth building is a regular grounding pass. After Cline finishes a batch, run the project tests and your linter, then read the diff once more with fresh eyes before you push. The point is not to distrust Cline; it is to make sure the tool's work is a proposal you have verified rather than an assumption you accepted. Over a few weeks this discipline turns Cline from something a skeptical reviewer fears into a dependable assistant whose judgment you trust because you check it.

Pros

  • Open-source and free — bring your own API key
  • Works with any model (Claude, GPT, Gemini, local models)
  • Integrates into existing VS Code workflow Autonomous multi-step execution saves significant time

Cons

  • Less polished than Cursor's agent mode
  • Can get confused on very large codebases
  • API costs add up on long autonomous sessions Requires manual approval for safety (or careful auto-approve settings)

Pricing

Cline itself is free and open-source. You pay for the underlying model API. A typical coding session with Claude Sonnet costs $0.50-2.00. With GPT-4o, about the same. With local models like DeepSeek Coder, effectively free after hardware costs.

Final Verdict

Cline is the best open-source AI coding agent available. It does not match Cursor's polish, but the model flexibility and zero licensing cost make it a compelling choice for developers who want AI agency without vendor lock-in. Rating: 7.5/10
