title: How Many Users Can Your VPS Actually Handle? A Practical Guide to Capacity Planning
summary:
Every developer knows this moment.

You just deployed a clean Laravel app on a $6 DigitalOcean Droplet. Everything feels fast. Then your client or your business lead sends a message: "Hey, we're launching a marketing campaign next week. How many people can use the site at once before it crashes?"

Most of us freeze for a second and guess. "Uh, maybe a few hundred? We can just upgrade the server if it gets slow."

Guessing works fine until it doesn't. If you overestimate, your site goes down right in the middle of a paid ad campaign. If you underestimate, you end up paying for a massive server you don't even need yet.

In the industry, solving this problem is called Capacity Planning. It sounds like a heavy enterprise buzzword, but you don't need expensive monitoring tools to do it. You can SSH into your VPS right now, run four safe commands, do three lines of simple math, and get a realistic answer in under five minutes.

Here is how to measure what your server can actually handle and how to turn those numbers into a real server budget.

Step 1: Pull Your Real Numbers From the Server

Before you calculate anything, you need to know what your server is doing right now. SSH into your VPS and run these four commands.

1. Check your CPU, RAM, and disk space 

echo "CPU Cores: $(nproc)" && free -m && df -h /

Look at the available RAM column (in MB) and your CPU core count. That available RAM is the main ceiling for how much traffic your server can take.

2. Check how much RAM each PHP-FPM worker uses

This is the most important number for a PHP or Laravel stack. Every incoming request needs a PHP worker to process it, and each worker eats a slice of your RAM.

ps aux | grep '[p]hp-fpm: pool' | awk '{sum+=$6; n++} END {if(n>0) printf "Active Workers: %d | Avg RAM/Worker: %.2f MB\n", n, sum/n/1024; else print "No workers found"}'

This tells you how many workers are currently running and the average megabytes each one consumes.

3. Check your Redis memory usage

If you use Redis for caching on the same VPS, you need to know how much RAM it's taking and whether it has a limit set.

redis-cli info memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory_human"

If maxmemory_human says 0B, it means Redis has no memory cap. Keep an eye on that an uncapped Redis instance can quietly eat into the RAM your app needs.

4. Measure your request processing time (TTFB)

Now, measure how long your server actually takes to generate a response. This is called Time to First Byte (TTFB).

Replace your-domain.com with your actual domain. Run it once on a light, cached page (your best-case scenario) and once on a heavy, database-driven page like a dashboard or search page (your worst-case scenario):

# Best-Case (light or cached page)
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "Best-Case -> Server Time (TTFB): %{time_starttransfer}s | Total: %{time_total}s\n" https://your-domain.com/

# Worst-Case (heavy or dynamic page)
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "Worst-Case -> Server Time (TTFB): %{time_starttransfer}s | Total: %{time_total}s\n" https://your-domain.com/heavy-page-url

Step 2: Do the Math Yourself

Once you have those four outputs, you don't need a black-box calculator. You can verify everything by hand in three steps.

1. Find your safe number of PHP workers ($W$)

Never plan to use 100% of your available RAM. Leave at least 20% as a safety buffer for the operating system, Nginx, and Redis. Divide the remaining 80% by the average RAM per PHP worker:

(Tip: If you only have 1 CPU core, don't push $W$ too high even if you have spare RAM too many workers fighting for one core will just slow everything down.)

2. Calculate Requests Per Second ($RPS$)

Divide your safe worker count by your server processing time (TTFB in seconds):

Run this twice:

  • Best-Case RPS: Use the TTFB from your light, cached page.
  • Worst-Case RPS: Use the TTFB from your heavy, dynamic page.

3. Estimate concurrent active users

Real people don't click a new link every single second. After a page loads, a user usually spends 5 to 10 seconds reading, scrolling, or filling out a form before clicking again. Performance engineers call this Think Time.

A quick real-world example

Think of your server like a small ticket counter.

Suppose your math gives you $W = 5$ workers (5 staff members behind the counter). If your app is well-cached and takes 0.2 seconds to handle a request:

If each visitor spends an average of 5 seconds reading a page before clicking again:

That means your small server can comfortably handle around 125 people browsing at the same time.

Now flip it to the worst case. If a heavy page with unoptimized database queries takes 1.0 second to load, your capacity drops to 5 RPS meaning only 25 to 50 active users before people start waiting in line and seeing 502 Bad Gateway errors.

Step 3: How Tech and Business Teams Turn This Into a Budget

Knowing your server's limit is great for debugging, but it becomes even more useful when you sit down with a business developer or client to plan server costs. Here is how experienced tech leads bridge the gap between terminal outputs and a budget spreadsheet:

  1. Start with a baseline: Use the math above to establish a clear benchmark for example, "Our current $6/month VPS comfortably handles 100 active users."
  2. Apply the 3x Peak Traffic Rule: If the business team expects 50 active users on a normal Tuesday, don't budget for 50. During a holiday sale, a viral post, or an ad push, traffic easily spikes to 3x the normal load (150 users). Always size your server for the peak, not the average.
  3. Stick to the 70% Safety Threshold: Never wait until your RAM or CPU hits 100% to upgrade. Plan your budget so that once sustained peak traffic crosses 70% of your server's capacity, you automatically move up to the next tier.
  4. Calculate Cost per Active User: Once you know your baseline, you can tell the business team exactly what it costs to support every 100 or 1,000 active users. That makes it easy for them to factor infrastructure costs directly into product pricing or marketing budgets.

Step 2: Do the Math Yourself

Once you have those four outputs, you don't need a black-box calculator. You can verify everything by hand in three steps.

1. Find your safe number of PHP workers ($W$)

Never plan to use 100% of your available RAM. Leave at least 20% as a safety buffer for the operating system, Nginx, and Redis. Divide the remaining 80% by the average RAM per PHP worker:

(Tip: If you only have 1 CPU core, don't push $W$ too high even if you have spare RAM too many workers fighting for one core will just slow everything down.)

2. Calculate Requests Per Second ($RPS$)

Divide your safe worker count by your server processing time (TTFB in seconds):

Run this twice:

  • Best-Case RPS: Use the TTFB from your light, cached page.
  • Worst-Case RPS: Use the TTFB from your heavy, dynamic page.

3. Estimate concurrent active users

Real people don't click a new link every single second. After a page loads, a user usually spends 5 to 10 seconds reading, scrolling, or filling out a form before clicking again. Performance engineers call this Think Time.

A quick real-world example

Think of your server like a small ticket counter.

Suppose your math gives you $W = 5$ workers (5 staff members behind the counter). If your app is well-cached and takes 0.2 seconds to handle a request:

If each visitor spends an average of 5 seconds reading a page before clicking again:

That means your small server can comfortably handle around 125 people browsing at the same time.

Now flip it to the worst case. If a heavy page with unoptimized database queries takes 1.0 second to load, your capacity drops to 5 RPS meaning only 25 to 50 active users before people start waiting in line and seeing 502 Bad Gateway errors.

Step 3: How Tech and Business Teams Turn This Into a Budget

Knowing your server's limit is great for debugging, but it becomes even more useful when you sit down with a business developer or client to plan server costs. Here is how experienced tech leads bridge the gap between terminal outputs and a budget spreadsheet:

  1. Start with a baseline: Use the math above to establish a clear benchmark for example, "Our current $6/month VPS comfortably handles 100 active users."
  2. Apply the 3x Peak Traffic Rule: If the business team expects 50 active users on a normal Tuesday, don't budget for 50. During a holiday sale, a viral post, or an ad push, traffic easily spikes to 3x the normal load (150 users). Always size your server for the peak, not the average.
  3. Stick to the 70% Safety Threshold: Never wait until your RAM or CPU hits 100% to upgrade. Plan your budget so that once sustained peak traffic crosses 70% of your server's capacity, you automatically move up to the next tier.
  4. Calculate Cost per Active User: Once you know your baseline, you can tell the business team exactly what it costs to support every 100 or 1,000 active users. That makes it easy for them to factor infrastructure costs directly into product pricing or marketing budgets.

title: PHP's November 2026 Security Release: How to Check, Patch and Restart (and What's New in PHP 8.6)
summary:
On November 19, 2026, PHP shipped PHP 8.6.0 and, on the same afternoon, security releases for every supported branch: 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36. The security releases fix 17 vulnerabilities, seven rated critical. PHP says the critical ones need non-default settings or uncommon setups, but several can lead to running code on the server.

The ones most likely to matter:

  • CVE-2026-129289, PHP-FPM request smuggling. If nginx (fastcgi_keep_conn on) or Apache (enablereuse=on) reuses FastCGI connections, leftover bytes from a request body can be read as a second, forged request that can run code. Standard setups that close the connection aren't affected by the demonstrated attack.
  • Three session bugs (CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-129481), including the upload-progress issue PHP warned about in October. Session upload progress is now off by default.
  • Two PHP 8.5-only bugs in the new fatal-error backtraces. The production setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1 blocks the demonstrated attack.
  • CVE-2026-129291, which can turn a compromised FPM worker into root when catch_workers_output is on, as it is in the official Docker images.

Check properly. Ubuntu and Debian backport fixes without changing the version, so a patched Ubuntu 24.04 still reports PHP 8.3.6. Look for the CVE in the package changelog instead: zcat /usr/share/doc/php*-common/changelog.Debian.gz | grep -m1 CVE-2026-129289. The fixed Ubuntu 24.04 package is 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.14.

Then update and restart PHP-FPM (or Apache for mod_php). Docker users should rebuild on the new php: images.

If you skipped October's release, this matters even more: the PHP2Shell bugs it fixed have been on CISA's list of exploited vulnerabilities since October 26, and this update covers them too.

PHP 8.6 brings partial function application, a \Time\Duration class, clamp(), a SortDirection enum and readonly property defaults. Patch first and test 8.6 later. The exception is PHP 8.2, whose support ends on December 31, 2026.

Sources

  • PHP: PHP 8.6.0 released and November 19 security releases
  • PHP 8 ChangeLog (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36)
  • PHP 8.6 release page
  • PHP supported versions
  • GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6: PHP-FPM request smuggling (CVE-2026-129289)
  • GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx: Session serializer mismatch (CVE-2026-115560)
  • GHSA-8mjj-2r7p-4hg2: Use-after-free in magic method backtraces (CVE-2026-129474)
  • GHSA-jm4m-qfqx-967m: PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free (CVE-2026-129291)
  • Ubuntu changelog: php8.3 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.14
  • Debian security tracker: CVE-2026-129289
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog

This is the short version. The full guide, with every step and source, is on GeekSpark.
